title: The resurrection of the body (CCC 988–1004)
hook: Catholics believe the whole person, body too, will be raised

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beatific vision: seeing God face to face. Your line was face to face. Who got your whole face? Today, the part of the Creed that says the face itself, and the body it belongs to, has a future too. Day three hundred twenty-nine.

A lot of people, if you ask them what happens after death, describe something like this: the soul floats free, like a bird out of a cage, and the body is left behind like an old coat. It's a very old idea, and it feels spiritual. But in the Apostles' Creed, just before the very last line, Christians say something much stranger and more physical. Not the survival of the soul. Something about bodies. Hands, faces, the scar on your knee. The Catholic Church says the coat isn't thrown away. Today, one of the boldest lines in the Creed.
screen: `A BIRD OUT OF A CAGE?` → `AN OLD COAT LEFT BEHIND?` → `HANDS, FACES, SCARS.`

segments.voice: First, the line. The old Prayer Book prints the Apostles' Creed's ending: "The Resurrection of the body, And the life everlasting." In Latin it's even blunter: carnis resurrectionem, the resurrection of the flesh. Second, why the body. The Catechism says a human being isn't a soul trapped in a body. We are one: body and soul together. So salvation isn't escape from the body. It's the whole person, raised. The early writer Tertullian made a Latin pun: caro salutis est cardo. The flesh is the hinge of salvation. Remember cardo, the hinge, from the four virtues? God took flesh, was raised in the flesh, and, Catholics say, will raise ours. Third, what kind of body. Not a corpse stitched back together. Paul compares it to a seed and the plant it becomes: the same life, utterly changed. In the Douay-Rheims: "It is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption." The Catechism says we'll rise with our own bodies, the ones we have now, but transformed, like Christ's risen body: real, recognizable, no longer able to die. How exactly, the Catechism says, goes beyond our imagination and understanding. When: on the last day, when Christ returns. Fourth, what it means for today. If the body has a future, it isn't disposable. Paul says "your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost." So Catholics are asked to respect their own bodies and everyone else's: the sick body, the aging body, the body in the grave. This week walked the last things: Mary, death, judgment, purgatory, hell, heaven, and now the body too.
screen: `CARNIS RESURRECTIONEM.` · `BODY AND SOUL, ONE PERSON.` · `CARO SALUTIS EST CARDO.` · `A SEED AND ITS PLANT.` · then, large: `SOWN IN CORRUPTION, RISEN IN INCORRUPTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat your body with gratitude. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet. They've carried you everywhere. Thank them. Your hands, that have held people. Your lungs, filling right now without being asked. Your heart, beating since before you were born. Notice any part that hurts, or that you've been unkind to in your head. Thank that part too. If you pray, you can thank God for the body you've been given. The bell holds the time.
The resurrection of the body. The Catholic belief that on the last day the whole person, body too, will be raised and transformed, like Christ. Today's word.
screen: `THE RESURRECTION OF THE BODY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the body too. Today, do one kind thing for your body: water, a walk, sleep, a meal eaten slowly. And one for someone else's. Day three hundred twenty-nine.
screen: `THIS WEEK: MARY · DEATH · JUDGMENT · PURGATORY · HELL · HEAVEN · THE BODY TOO`

howItsDone: Catholics profess the resurrection of the body in the Creed, bury their dead or reverently inter their ashes in consecrated places rather than scattering them, and honor the body in funeral rites as one day to be raised.

original.note: Latin, the Apostles' Creed: the resurrection of the flesh.

trapdoor: what you thought: after death the soul floats free of the body.
what it means: Catholics believe the whole person, body and soul, will be raised on the last day, transformed like Christ.
what a scholar hears: carnis resurrectionem; Tertullian's caro salutis est cardo; 1 Corinthians 15:35–44's soma pneumatikon; CCC 997–1001.
